behavior.description: The Garibaldi, known historically as the Catalina goldfish and marine goldfish and now commonly as the Garibaldi damselfish, is a species of bright orange fish in the damselfish family. It occurs in the subtropical northeastern part of the Pacific Ocean. The Garibaldi was named the official marine state fish of California in 1995, and has since been protected in California coastal waters from recreation and commercial fishing.

sections.section_description: Garibaldi are deep-bodied or laterally compressed fish, and covered in coarse scales. They have a single dorsal fin with about 12 spines and 16 rays.[5]Adult fish of this species are uniformly bright orange in color. It is the largest member of thedamselfishfamily growing up to 35.6 cm (14 inches) in length. Among Garibaldi there is a sexual size dimorphism, with average adult males measuring 25mm (1 inch) larger than females,[6]⁠—an unusual trait for damselfish species and other marine fish in
sections.section_biology: The breeding season for Garibaldi may begin as early as March and continue through July.[5]During this time, the male clears a sheltered nest site within his territory, and then the female deposits eggs in the nest. When first deposited, the elliptical eggs are bright yellow and turn gray after approximately 5 days.[9]After fertilizing the eggs, the male guards the nest area until the eggs hatch, which takes 19–21 days. sections.section_diet: Classified as generalist omnivores, Garibaldi feed mainly oninvertebrates,[4]which they remove from the rocks. Their diet also includes a variety of algae and occasionally their own eggs.[3]Garibaldi are found to most commonly feed upon fleshy red algae,polychaeteworms, anemones, and sponge fragments.
